key_insight: An EHR-based machine learning model for peripheral artery disease showed fairly consistent performance across five health systems, but accuracy varied by patient phenotype.
clinical_relevance: This suggests PAD screening tools may be more useful when evaluated not just by overall metrics, but also by patient subgroups and care-setting differences.
method: 33,739 PAD cases were matched to 33,739 controls from the University of California Health Data Warehouse.
A LightGBM model used 14,023 EHR features, including demographics, comorbidities, medications, labs, utilization, and coded diagnoses/procedures.
Unsupervised clustering defined four PAD phenotypes, and model performance plus fairness were assessed across institutions and subgroups.
evidence_signal: Overall discrimination was consistent across sites (AUROC 0.76–0.79; AUC-PR 0.76–0.79) with good calibration, but sensitivity ranged from 0.40 in the limited-documentation cluster to 0.87 in the severe-metabolic-disease cluster.
watch_item: The weakest performance in patients with limited healthcare documentation highlights a risk that EHR-based models may be less reliable in under-captured populations.
paper_title: Performance and Fairness of a Peripheral Artery Disease Detection Model Across Patient Phenotypes and Health Systems
